unit.title: Carry out data entry and retrieval procedures

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how you would design a spreadsheet or database table to record the inspection and test results for every circuit in a building, so that data can be keyed quickly and correctly.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the test sheet and the certificate the firm issues, and list every item to be recorded. Each item becomes one field with a clear heading: job number, board, circuit number, description, breaker type and rating, cable size, R1+R2, insulation resistance, RCD trip time, polarity, result and tester's name and date. One row holds one circuit. I would set the right data type for each field: numbers for readings in one stated unit, dates for dates, and text for serial numbers. I would add validation: drop-down lists for breaker ratings and Pass or Fail, range checks on readings, a required job number and a format check on IDs. Fields would be in the same order as the paper sheet so keying flows. I would protect the headings and formulas, add a unique ID for each record, and test the design with a few sample sheets before it is used.
markingPoints: Lists the fields from the test sheet and certificate, one row per circuit
Sets the right data type and units for each field
Adds validation: drop-downs, range checks, required fields, format checks
Orders fields to match the source document
Protects the layout, uses a unique ID and tests the design first

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would build into a form for keying circuit test results, and the checks that a person must still make. Give examples using test data.
essays.modelAnswer: A form can check that data is sensible as it is keyed. A presence check makes sure the job number and circuit number are never left blank. A range check stops an insulation reading of minus 5 or a trip time of 50 000 ms. A format check makes sure job numbers follow the firm's pattern, such as J and four digits. Drop-down lists make sure breaker ratings and results are chosen, not typed in many spellings. A look-up can warn when a 2.5 mm² cable is entered on a 40 A breaker. But a form cannot tell whether a sensible number is the true one. If the sheet says 25 MΩ and the clerk keys 250 MΩ, the form accepts it. So a person must verify the data: compare the keyed batch with the paper sheets, or have a second person check each entry, or key it twice and compare. The tester should also review the finished schedule before the certificate is signed.
markingPoints: Presence check example
Range check example with test data
Format checks, drop-downs or warnings for odd combinations
Explains that validation cannot catch a wrong but sensible value
Describes verification: checking against source, second person, double keying, tester review

essays.stem: Describe how you would key in a stack of 40 handwritten site test sheets from a school rewiring job, from receiving them to filing them, and how you would make sure the data is right.
essays.modelAnswer: When the sheets arrive I would count them, check that each has a job number, board, date and the tester's name, and log their receipt. I would look through for gaps, unclear figures or readings that look wrong and list them as queries for the tester, rather than guessing. I would sort the sheets into board and circuit order so they match the file. Then I would key them in batches, saving often, using the number pad, and following the firm's procedure for units and abbreviations. After each batch I would check the screen or a print against the sheets, or have a second person check them, and compare totals such as the number of circuits. When the tester answers the queries I would update those records and note the change. Last, I would mark each sheet as entered with the date and my initials, and file the sheets by job number so they can be found later.
markingPoints: Counts and logs the sheets and checks they are complete
Lists unclear or doubtful entries as queries instead of guessing
Sorts the sheets and keys in batches, saving often, following the procedure
Verifies each batch against the sheets or by a second person
Updates after queries, marks sheets as entered and files them

essays.stem: A hotel's maintenance manager asks which emergency lights, fire alarm devices and RCDs are due for testing next month. Explain how you would get this information from the asset file and present it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make sure I have the latest version of the asset register and that the due-date field is a real date for every item. If the register only holds the last test date, I would add a column that works out the next due date from the test interval for each type of item. Then I would filter the register: the item type set to emergency light, fire alarm device or RCD, and the due date set to between the first and last day of next month. I would sort the result by location, such as building, floor and room, so the electricians can plan their rounds, and then by item type. I would use COUNTIF or a pivot table to give a total for each type. The report would have a clear title, the date it was run, the filter used, and the list with the asset ID, location, type and due date. I would check a few items against the register, then save it as a PDF and send it to the manager.
markingPoints: Uses the latest register and checks the due-date data
Works out next due dates if only last test dates are held
Filters by item type and next month's date range
Sorts by location and totals by type
Presents a clear, titled, dated, checked report (such as a PDF)

essays.stem: Explain how an electrical contractor should protect its client and job data, including its duties under Jamaica's data protection law.
essays.modelAnswer: Client records hold names, addresses, phone numbers and sometimes alarm codes or details of a home's layout, so they must be protected. Jamaica's data protection law says personal data must be collected for a clear purpose, kept accurate, kept no longer than needed, kept secure and used fairly, and people have rights to know what is held about them. In practice, each worker should have their own login with a strong password, and access should match their job, so only managers can delete records. Screens should lock when staff leave them, and laptops, tablets and phones should be encrypted and protected with a PIN. Backups should be kept safe as well. Client data should never be shared with other firms or callers without a proper reason and approval. Paper sheets should be locked away and shredded when no longer needed. Staff should be trained to spot scam emails and report any loss of data quickly to the manager.
markingPoints: Explains why client data is sensitive
States the general duties of the data protection law (purpose, accuracy, security, fair use, rights)
Own logins, strong passwords, access by role, screen locks
Encrypts mobile devices, protects backups and paper records
No sharing without reason; staff trained; losses reported

essays.stem: Explain how an electrical contractor should back up and archive its job records and certificates, and why they may be needed years later.
essays.modelAnswer: Job records and certificates should be backed up at least every working day, automatically if possible. One copy should be kept away from the office, for example on a cloud service or a drive taken home by the manager, so a fire, flood, theft or computer failure does not destroy everything. Backups should be checked now and then by restoring a file to make sure they work. When a job is finished, its records, drawings, test results, certificates and photos should be moved to an archive folder named by job number, in a format that will still open later, such as PDF. The archive is kept for as long as the firm's policy and the law require, then disposed of securely. Records may be needed years later when the client sells the building, when an inspector or insurer asks for proof, when a fault or fire is investigated, when an extension is added or when the firm must defend its work in a dispute.
markingPoints: Regular (daily) backups, automatic where possible
A copy kept off-site or online
Backups tested by restoring
Finished jobs archived by job number in a lasting format, kept per policy
Gives reasons records are needed later (sale, inspection, investigation, extension, dispute)

essays.stem: You find that a batch of downloaded test results was matched to the wrong distribution board. Explain how you would correct the records, keep an audit trail and stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would stop anyone using those results, and check whether any certificate has already been issued from them. I would find the source: the tester's file and the site sheets for both boards. I would back up the file before changing anything. Then I would move each result to the right board and circuit, checking each one against the source, and check that the other board's own results are still correct. The database's change log, or a note in a corrections register, would record what was changed, by whom, when and why. If a certificate had been issued, it would be withdrawn and a corrected one issued, and the client told. To stop it happening again, I would find the cause, for example the tester saved two boards under one name. I would add a step to the procedure: the board ID must be set on the tester before testing, and the office checks it against the site sheet when downloading.
markingPoints: Stops use of the wrong results and checks for issued certificates
Backs up, then corrects each record against the source
Records what changed, by whom, when and why
Withdraws and reissues any certificate and informs the client
Finds the cause and changes the procedure to prevent it

essays.stem: Compare keying test results by hand with downloading them from a test instrument or entering them on a tablet on site. Give the benefits, the risks and the checks needed for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Keying by hand from paper sheets needs no special equipment and leaves a paper record, but it is slow, and every figure can be misread or mistyped, so it needs careful verification against the sheets. Downloading from a test instrument is fast and removes keying errors, because the reading goes straight from the tester. The risks are that results are saved under the wrong board or circuit on the tester, that a file is overwritten, or that the software does not match the tester's version. The office must check that each result is matched to its circuit and that the instrument was in calibration. Entering on a tablet on site lets the form check data at once and send it to the office the same day. The risks are a lost or stolen tablet, a flat battery or no signal, and a rushed entry. Tablets need a screen lock and encryption, a backup sync, and a review by the tester before the certificate is signed.
markingPoints: Hand keying: simple, paper record, but slow and error-prone; needs verification
Download: fast, fewer keying errors
Download risks: wrong board or circuit, overwritten files; check matching and calibration
Tablet: checks at entry, quick sending
Tablet risks and controls: loss, battery, signal; lock, encryption, sync, review

essays.stem: Explain how you would produce a monthly report for the manager from the job database, showing jobs completed, hours and materials per job, and failed tests, and how you would check it before sending.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure all of the month's timesheets, material issues and test results had been keyed in before running the report. Then I would run a query or filter for jobs completed between the first and last day of the month. For each job I would total the hours from the timesheets and the materials cost from the issues, using a pivot table or SUMIF, and list any circuits whose tests failed, with the job, board and circuit. I would lay the report out with a title, the period, a short summary of totals at the top, then the table by job, and a chart if it helps. Before sending it I would check the totals against the source in a few places, check that no job is missing or counted twice, compare it with last month for anything odd, and make sure it holds no client data the manager does not need. Then I would save it as a PDF with a clear file name and send it.
markingPoints: Makes sure all data for the month is entered first
Uses a query or filter for the month's completed jobs
Totals hours and materials per job and lists failed tests
Clear layout: title, period, summary, table, chart
Checks totals against source, missing or double entries, odd changes; sends as PDF

essays.stem: As office supervisor, describe how you would set up and run data entry for a team of three clerks, so that the work is accurate, on time and consistent.
essays.modelAnswer: I would write a short procedure for each kind of record, such as test results, timesheets and stock issues, with the field rules, units, abbreviations and an example, and train each clerk on it. I would set up the files with validation and drop-down lists so they all enter data the same way, and give each clerk their own login with rights that suit their work. I would agree deadlines, such as test results keyed within two working days, and share the work out fairly, with a log of which batches each clerk has. Each batch would be verified, either by the clerk against the sheets or by another clerk checking a sample. I would check a sample myself each week, look at the error rate for each clerk, and coach anyone who needs it. Queries would go back to the site through one route. I would make sure backups run, review the procedure when problems recur, and make sure the workstations are set up well and breaks are taken.
markingPoints: Written procedure with field rules and examples; staff trained
Files set up with validation; own logins and suitable rights
Deadlines set and work shared and logged
Verification of batches and supervisor sampling with coaching
Query route, backups, procedure review and workstation welfare

practical1.title: Design a circuit test-results file and key in a batch of site test sheets
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group 20 handwritten site test sheets for two distribution boards in a made-up clinic in May Pen. Some sheets have planted problems: unclear figures, a missing circuit number, a reading in the wrong unit and a duplicated circuit. As a data team: (1) agree the fields, their order, data types and units, and build the table in a spreadsheet or database; (2) add validation: drop-down lists for breaker rating and result, range checks on the readings and a required job number; (3) list every unclear or doubtful entry on a query sheet instead of guessing; (4) share the sheets out, and each member keys their share; (5) each member verifies another member's share against the sheets and corrects errors, noting each correction; (6) filter out the failed or doubtful circuits into a short summary for the 'tester' (the assessor), and save the file with a clear name and a backup copy. Photograph the screen at each stage and the query sheet.
materials: 20 handwritten test sheets for two boards (made-up data, from the assessor)
Computers with a spreadsheet or database program, one for each member if possible
A USB drive or shared folder for the backup copy
Query sheet and correction log forms
A phone or camera for photos of the screen
photos: The agreed field list with data types and units
The empty table with validation set up (drop-down list showing)
The query sheet listing unclear or doubtful entries
Each member's keyed share on screen
The filtered summary of failed or doubtful circuits and the saved file names
checklist: Helped choose sensible fields, data types and units
Set up at least one working validation rule
Queried unclear entries instead of guessing
Keyed their share accurately in the agreed format
Verified another member's share and logged corrections
Used a filter or query correctly to pick out failed circuits
Saved with a clear file name and made a backup
safety: Sit with good posture, screen at eye level, and take short breaks from the screen
Keep drinks away from the computers and cables off the walkways
Treat the client and test data as confidential, even though it is made up
Lock or log off the computer when you leave it

practical2.title: Retrieve maintenance data from an asset register and report to the manager
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group an electronic asset register (about 200 rows) for a made-up hotel in Ocho Rios: emergency lights, RCDs, distribution boards, motors and portable equipment, with locations, last test dates, test intervals and results. Some rows have planted problems: a duplicate board, a date stored as text and a missing location. As a team: (1) back up the file before changing it; (2) find and fix the planted problems, writing each change in a change log; (3) work out the next due date for each item; (4) filter for items due next month and sort them by location; (5) use COUNTIF or a pivot table to total items due and items that failed, by type; (6) produce a one-page report with a title, date, summary table and chart, and save it as a PDF; (7) email or share it with the 'manager' (the assessor). Each member does at least one of steps 2 to 6 at the keyboard while another member checks the result. Photograph the screen at each step.
materials: Asset register file with about 200 rows (made-up data, from the assessor)
A shared folder or USB drive for the backup
An email account or shared folder set up by the Centre
A phone or camera for photos of the screen
photos: The backup copy saved, with its file name
The planted problems found, and the change log
The next due date column with its formula
The filtered and sorted list of items due next month
The COUNTIF results or pivot table
The finished one-page report as a PDF and the sent email
checklist: Made a backup before changing the file
Found and fixed planted problems and logged each change
Wrote a correct formula for the next due date
Filtered and sorted the data correctly
Totalled by type with COUNTIF or a pivot table
Produced a clear, titled, dated report and saved it as a PDF
Checked another member's step and sent the report correctly
safety: Sit with good posture and take short screen breaks
Keep drinks away from computers and cables off the floor
Keep the register and report confidential; send only to the named person
Lock or log off the computer when you leave it
